concept.name: Reservoir Sampling

relationships.description: Connects Reservoir Sampling to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

concept.tagline: Selecting a uniform random sample of k items from an unbounded stream of unknown length n in one pass and O(k) memory.
concept.purpose: Build a progressive mental model of reservoir sampling—from Vitter's Algorithm R and $O(k(1 + \log(n/k)))$ Algorithm L skips to weighted Efraimidis-Spirakis and distributed min-heap merges.

spark.summary: Reservoir sampling selects a uniformly random sample of k items from a data stream of unknown or unbounded length n in a single pass using O(k) memory.
spark.keyTakeaway: Maintain a fixed k-element array and accept the i-th incoming item (i > k) with probability k/i, replacing a random slot—giving every item an exact k/n selection probability without knowing n upfront.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** **Reservoir sampling** solves a core streaming constraint: picking $k$ items uniformly at random from a stream of unknown length $n$ in **one pass** and **$O(k)$ RAM**.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts Single-Pass O(k) Reservoir Updates on Stream A, B, C, D, E (Event Stream -> PRNG j in [1..i] -> Reservoir[0..2]); Per-Shard Min-Heap -> Global Top-K Priority Merge (Global Top-K Heap -> Shard 1 (1M ev/m) -> Shard 2 (10k ev/m) -> Key = log(u)/w).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Compare CPU cost, memory predictability, and distributed mergeability. Each of 16 Kafka consumer workers runs a local $O(k)$ min-heap keyed by `u = rng.random()` (or `log(u)/w`).

**Failure Modes & Application:** Explore randomized algorithms, tail-based APM sampling, and streaming pipelines.

learningJourney.title: What is Reservoir Sampling (Algorithm R & Algorithm L)
learningJourney.explanation:
**Reservoir sampling** solves a core streaming constraint: picking $k$ items uniformly at random from a stream of unknown length $n$ in **one pass** and **$O(k)$ RAM**.

In **Vitter's Algorithm R**, you store the first $k$ items, then for each $i > k$ (1-indexed), draw random $j \in [1, i]$; if $j \le k$, overwrite `reservoir[j-1]`. By induction, every item has exact probability $k/n$. **Algorithm L** speeds this up from $O(n)$ to $O(k(1 + \log(n/k)))$ by sampling geometric skip distances.

sectionDiagram.title: Single-Pass O(k) Reservoir Updates on Stream A, B, C, D, E
sectionDiagram.summary: After 5 items, every element {A,B,C,D,E} had an exact 3/5 probability of ending up in the reservoir.

learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Reservoir Sampling (Algorithm R & Algorithm L) works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Why we need Reservoir Sampling (and Distributed Merge Traps)
learningJourney.explanation: Telemetry agents, Kafka consumers, and `PostgreSQL ANALYZE` cannot buffer billions of rows or run two passes. Two subtle traps break naive implementations: (1) **Biased Distributed Merge**: concatenating $k$ items from a 1M-event shard and a 10k-event shard over-represents the quiet shard by 100x; (2) **Stale History**: in an infinite daemon, after 10B events, new items have $k/10^{10}$ entry probability unless tumbled or time-decayed.

ideas.title: Weighted & Mergeable Keys: `log(u) / w`
ideas.description: Efraimidis-Spirakis assigns each item a key $u^{1/w}$ (compute `log(u) / w` to avoid floating-point underflow) and keeps the top $k$ in a min-heap—enabling exact distributed merges!

ideas.title: Avoid `crypto/rand` Inside Hot Loops
ideas.description: Use fast thread-local PRNGs (`xoshiro256**`, `PCG64`) and switch to Algorithm L when $n \gg k$.

learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Reservoir Sampling under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Where Reservoir Sampling fits (and where Stratified/Index Sampling wins)
learningJourney.explanation: Use reservoir sampling for unbounded streams with strict RAM caps; use index sampling on static tables or stratified/tail-based sampling for rare anomalies.

benefits: Strict $O(k)$ memory immune to traffic spikes and exact uniform coverage without knowing $n$.
costs: Destroys temporal arrival order unless `(arrival_seq, item)` is stored and sorted on readout.

benefits: Use **stratified** or **tail-based sampling** so 100% of errors are kept instead of drowned out by 99.9% `200 OK`s.
costs: Uniform sampling drops rare anomalies proportionally.

benefits: Use `TABLESAMPLE` or direct index offsets without scanning every row.
costs: Algorithm R still reads all $n$ elements.

learningJourney.explanation: Use unbiased integer range generation (`random.randrange`), verify uniformity with chi-squared tests over 100k trials, and use `log(u) / w` min-heaps for weighted or multi-shard distributed streams.
learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Alternatives: Algorithm R vs. Algorithm L vs. Hash-Modulo Threshold
learningJourney.explanation: Compare CPU cost, memory predictability, and distributed mergeability.

benefits: 10 lines of integer code, $O(k)$ exact RAM.

costs: Slightly more floating-point math for geometric skip calculation.

benefits: Stateless and trivially parallel across workers.
costs: Produces variable-size output that blows memory budgets during 10x traffic spikes.

learningJourney.purpose: The trade-off: compare competing approaches across latency, consistency, and operational cost.

learningJourney.title: Production example: Distributed Top-K Heap Merge Across Kafka Partitions
learningJourney.explanation: Each of 16 Kafka consumer workers runs a local $O(k)$ min-heap keyed by `u = rng.random()` (or `log(u)/w`). Every minute, workers emit their $k$-element heaps to an aggregator that takes the global top-$k$ keys—producing a mathematically unbiased global sample regardless of partition traffic skew.

sectionDiagram.title: Per-Shard Min-Heap -> Global Top-K Priority Merge

cards.label: 1. Scale-Invariant
cards.detail: Higher-traffic shards naturally draw larger max-keys, correcting for 100x skew automatically.

cards.label: 2. Bounded Memory
cards.detail: Every worker and aggregator stays strictly within O(k) RAM.

cards.label: 3. Tumbling Epochs
cards.detail: Reset heaps hourly so recent stream distributions are never drowned by ancient history.

knowledgeCheck.question: If Shard A processes 1,000,000 events and Shard B processes 10,000 events, why is uniformly sampling k items from their concatenated k-element reservoirs biased?

options.text: It gives Shard B's events 100x higher selection weight than Shard A's events; you must weight by shard count or merge via random priority keys
options.feedback: Correct: assigning each item a random key `u ~ Uniform(0,1)` and merging via a global top-k min-heap stays completely unbiased.

options.text: Because Algorithm R requires knowing total `n` before starting
options.feedback: Algorithm R does not need `n` upfront, only merging requires shard-size weighting or priority keys.

options.text: Because O(k) memory overflows when merging two arrays
options.feedback: Merging two k-element heaps still uses O(k) memory.

beginner.byteSummary:

**How It Flows:** Think of Reservoir Sampling as a clear step-by-step chain: Event Stream -> PRNG j in [1..i] -> Reservoir[0..2] -> Global Top-K Heap -> Shard 1 (1M ev/m).

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
